## Section 1 — Hero (`#top`)

**On-screen layout:** Two-column hero. Left: kicker + title + blurb + links. Right: giant “451×” metric.

- Kicker: STANFORD HPC · SUMMER 2026
- Title: AlphaFold / on TPU
- Body: “We timed the same AlphaFold JAX forward pass on CPU, GPU (T4), and TPU (v5e-8). At steady-state the TPU is 451× faster than CPU.”
- Links: Structure · Results · Reproduce
- Metric label: STEADY-STATE VS CPU
- Metric: **451×** (teal ×)
- Subline: TPU 0.47s · GPU 13.1s (16.2×) · CPU 212s
- Footer credit line under a hairline rule: Lorenzo Pazienza & Ihab El Bani · Intro to HPC and AI Systems · Profs. Steve Jones & Mourad Bouache

**Important:** GPU speedup vs CPU is **16.2×**. TPU vs GPU is ~27.8×. Do not say GPU is 27.8× vs CPU.

---

## Section 2 — Structure (`#structure`)

**Headline:** Human ubiquitin  
**Supporting:** ESMFold prediction · 76 residues · mean pLDDT **90.5**. Drag to rotate, scroll to zoom. Colors follow AlphaFold’s pLDDT scale.

### Media A — Interactive 3D viewer
- Asset (fallback still): https://alphafold-tpu.vercel.app/figures/ubiquitin_structure.png
- PDB: https://alphafold-tpu.vercel.app/structure/ubiquitin_predicted.pdb
- **What it shows:** Cartoon ribbon of human ubiquitin. Residues colored by pLDDT confidence:
  - >90 deep blue (very high)
  - 70–90 cyan (high)
  - 50–70 yellow (medium)
  - <50 orange (low)
- Most of the fold is blue/cyan (high confidence). The flexible C-terminal conjugating tail (roughly residues 71–76) is warmer / lower confidence.
- Caption note: “Lower confidence at the C-terminus (residues ~71–76)”

### Media B — Per-residue pLDDT line chart
- Also available as still: https://alphafold-tpu.vercel.app/figures/ubiquitin_confidence.png
- **What it shows:** Line chart, X = residue 1–76, Y = pLDDT ~40–100. Teal line stays high (~90–96) through the core, with a shaded band highlighting residues 70–76 where confidence drops (toward ~50s–70s at the end).
- Caption: “Shaded band: residues 70–76”
- Chart title on page: “Per-residue pLDDT” · mean 90.5

**Scope note (stated on site):** This ubiquitin fold is **biology / ESMFold with trained weights**. It is **not** the timed CPU/GPU/TPU systems workload (that uses Haiku random init on a 118-residue systems input).

---

## Section 3 — Problem (`#problem`)

- Kicker: Problem
- Headline: “Where does AlphaFold spend time on CPU, GPU, and TPU?”
- Body: Protein structure prediction is a real JAX/Haiku workload. Same model config, same script, same input shape on three backends; measure init, first predict (compile + run), and steady-state predict.
- Hardware note: Colab CPU and T4 for baselines; Stanford class cluster TPU v5e-8 (2×4) for TPU numbers and scaling sweeps.

---

## Section 4 — Approach (`#approach`)

- Kicker: Approach
- Headline: “One script, three backends”
- Body: Every timing run calls `spike_tpu_forward_pass.py`. Only the accelerator changes.

**Architecture strip (4 cells):**
1. Script — `spike_tpu_forward_pass.py`
2. CPU — Colab / local → `result_cpu.json`
3. GPU — Colab T4 → `result_gpu-t4.json`
4. TPU — Stanford v5e-8 → `result_tpu + traces`

**Parameters note:** Systems timings use Haiku random init to exercise the same compiled graph without downloading trained weights (~350MB). Ubiquitin above is separate (ESMFold).

---

## Section 5 — Results (`#results`)

- Kicker: Results
- Headline: “Steady-state predict latency”
- Big callout: **0.47s**
- Subcopy: model_3, 0 recycles, 118-residue input, identical code path. Bar lengths are log-scaled.

**Latency bars (log-scaled widths on page):**
| Backend | Display time | Speedup vs CPU | Bar color (approx) |
|---------|--------------|----------------|--------------------|
| CPU     | 212.1s       | 1×             | gray               |
| GPU T4  | 13.1s        | 16.2×          | blue               |
| TPU v5e | 0.47s        | 451×           | teal               |

**First predict / steady-state (compile visibility):**
| Backend | Ratio | Note |
|---------|-------|------|
| CPU     | 1.28× | Mostly compute |
| GPU T4  | 7.46× | Compile is visible |
| TPU v5e | 59.1× | Cold path is compile |

---

## Section 6 — Experiments (`#experiments`)

- Kicker: Experiments
- Headline: “Eleven TPU follow-ups”
- UX note on page: Click + on a row for method notes. Shared figures sit under each phase. Amber rail = negative result.

### Phase: Scaling

#### 01 Sequence length — **14.6×** (time for 8.3× length)
- Finding: Steady-state time grew faster than sequence length (8.3× length → 14.6× time).
- Notes: Swept 60, 120, 250, 500 residues. Super-linear; matches pair representation. Compile ~flat.

#### 02 Recycle depth — **~0.46s** (per extra recycle)
- Finding: Steady-state rose linearly with recycles; compile did not.
- Notes: 0/1/3 recycles; ~0.46s each added recycle. Compile jumps 0→1 then flat 1→3.

#### 03 Chip visibility — **1 of 8** (chips used)
- Finding: 1 visible chip and 8 visible chips gave the same single-query time.
- Notes: Default path one query on one chip. 2-/4-chip libtpu flag attempts failed.

### Media C — Shared scaling charts
- URL: https://alphafold-tpu.vercel.app/figures/scaling_charts.png
- Caption: “Left: sequence length. Right: recycle depth. Same TPU v5e-8 runs.”
- **What it shows:** Two side-by-side line charts for TPU v5e-8. Left: latency vs sequence length; right: latency vs recycle depth (118 residues). Each panel plots orange “compile + run (1st call)” and blue “steady-state (2nd call)”. Orange sits much higher; blue rises with length/recycles more gently.

### Phase: Bottleneck & fix

#### 04 Profiler trace — **76%** (of first call in cache_miss)
- Finding: cache_miss in JAX pjit accounted for ~76% of the first predict call.
- Notes: `$pjit.py:250` ~12.55s self-time inside 16.56s first predict; TPU device nearly idle → host-side JIT.

#### 05 Compilation cache — **6.8×** (faster init_params)
- Finding: Persisting JAX compile cache across process restart cut init_params by 6.8×.
- Notes: First predict also ~1.9× with warm cache; steady-state unchanged.

#### 06 Precision (bf16) — **−40%** (steady-state HBM)
- Finding: bfloat16 cut steady-state HBM ~40% with little runtime change at this size.
- Notes: Wall-clock barely moved; peak memory briefly higher during cast.

### Phase: Multi-chip

#### 07 Multi-query batching — **lower** (proteins/sec vs batch=1) · NEGATIVE
- Finding: jax.vmap reduced proteins/sec as batch size grew; only TPU_0 used HBM.
- Notes: Batches 1/2/4/8; throughput never beat batch=1; memory stayed on one chip.

### Media D — Batching chart
- URL: https://alphafold-tpu.vercel.app/figures/batching_chart.png
- Caption: “Wall-clock scales ~linearly; per-protein cost rises with batch size.”
- **What it shows:** Chart of batching experiment outcomes: as batch size increases, wall-clock grows roughly linearly and per-protein efficiency worsens versus batch=1; reinforces that vmap did not spread work across the 8-chip slice.

#### 08 pmap parallelism — **6.92×** (throughput speedup)
- Finding: jax.pmap ran 8 proteins on 8 chips at 6.92× single-chip throughput.
- Notes: 2.13 → 14.72 proteins/sec; per-chip HBM 445–469 MB ≈ single-protein footprint.

#### 09 Auto-sharding (GSPMD) — **0×** (tensor split) · NEGATIVE
- Finding: GSPMD auto-mesh left a full ~463 MB copy on every chip (no split).
- Notes: Reproduced twice; without sharding annotations AlphaFold replicated.

### Phase: Fit & rigor

#### 10 Empirical scaling law — **R² 0.981** (16-point TPU grid)
- Finding: Power law on 16 TPU runs (4 chip counts × 4 lengths) fits R² 0.981.
- Equation: throughput ≈ 4527.77 · chips^0.963 · length^−1.572
- Implication: chip exponent near 1 → pmap scaling holds; cost/prediction nearly flat in chips.

### Media E — Scaling law chart
- URL: https://alphafold-tpu.vercel.app/figures/scaling_law_chart.png
- Caption: “Throughput vs chips and sequence length on the measured grid.”
- **What it shows:** Visualization of the 16-run grid / fit: throughput rising with chip count and falling with sequence length, consistent with the fitted power law (R² 0.981).

#### 11 Model pick & repeats — **<1%** (stdev on repeats)
- Finding: model_5 ~15% faster at steady-state; three repeats stayed under 1% stdev.
- Notes: model_5 beat model_3 and model_4 by ~15%; all tracked metrics <1% stdev across three repeats.

---

## Section 7 — Cost (`#cost`)

- Kicker: Cost
- Headline: “Cost per prediction is nearly flat in chip count”
- Body: Choose chips for latency or throughput; do not expect lower unit cost from a larger slice.

**Formula block:**
- Label: Empirical fit · 16 TPU runs · R² 0.981
- throughput ≈ 4527.77 · chips^0.963 · length^−1.572
- Grid: chips {1,2,4,8} × length {100,250,500,1000}

**Dark callout band:**
On the baseline path only 1 of 8 chips was active (~87% idle), so list-price TPU and GPU land almost together: $1.25 vs $1.27 per 1k predictions. After pmap uses the full slice, cost per prediction stays roughly constant as chip count grows.

**Cost per 1,000 predictions (centered trio):**
| Backend     | Cost / 1k |
|-------------|-----------|
| CPU         | $11.19    |
| GPU T4      | $1.27     |
| TPU 8-chip  | $1.25     |

---

## Section 8 — Reproduce (`#reproduce`)

- Kicker: Reproduce
- Headline: “Code and commands”
- Body: Docker builds for CPU/GPU and Kubernetes manifests for the class TPU cluster are in the repo.
- Link: https://github.com/lorenzopazienza/alphafold-tpu-benchmark

**Repo layout table:**
| Path | Description |
|------|-------------|
| configs/ | Kubernetes job manifests |
| src/ | Benchmark script used on all backends |
| notebooks/ | Colab CPU, GPU, and ESMFold fold |
| figures/ | Charts referenced on this page |
| structure/ | Ubiquitin PDB |
| profiling/ | XLA trace notes |
| results/ | Per-run JSON, comparison, sweep/ |
| website/ | This site |

**CPU example (on page):**
```
docker build --build-arg JAX_VARIANT=cpu \
  -t af-bench:cpu .
docker run -v $(pwd)/results:/alphafold/results \
  af-bench:cpu --run_tag=cpu
```
GPU/TPU variants and Colab notebooks are in the README; sweep jobs under configs/.

## How to answer users about this site

1. Read this file end-to-end; treat it as the page content.
2. Separate **systems timing** (118-res, random init, CPU/GPU/TPU) from **ubiquitin ESMFold** (biology demo).
3. Quote the tables for latency, compile ratios, costs, and experiment stats.
4. Mention amber/negative results: batching (vmap) and GSPMD auto-shard.
5. Link people to the live section anchors (#structure, #results, #experiments, #cost, #reproduce) or the GitHub repo for code.
